title: Entanglement manipulation and magic area-laws
abstract: Physical many-body quantum systems typically interact locally, giving rise to ground states where entanglement grows with the area of the region being probed. Beyond entanglement, non-stabilizerness (or "magic") has been established as another crucial resource linked to quantum complexity and the properties of error-correcting states. Unlike entanglement, non-stabilizerness typically behaves with a volume-law scaling in ground states, indicating inherent computational complexity. In this work, we show that under a recent classification of quantum states, area-law states split into two distinct classes. Entanglement-dominated states obey an area-law for non-stabilizerness and admit efficient quantum algorithms for entanglement manipulation. Conversely, magic-dominated states exhibit a a faster-than-area growth of subsystem non-stabilizerness and require non-efficient algorithms for entanglement manipulation tasks. Within this context, we introduce the concept of the stabilizer regime, a restricted quantum phase that admits efficient entanglement manipulation and hosts area laws for both magic and entanglement.

bite.hook: Area-law quantum states split into classes where magic-dominated states show faster-than-area growth of non-stabilizerness.
tldr: Examined how non-stabilizerness (magic) scales in physical many-body quantum systems alongside entanglement.
Classified area-law quantum states into entanglement-dominated and magic-dominated categories.
Demonstrated that entanglement-dominated states allow efficient algorithms, while magic-dominated states require inefficient ones.
bite.whyItMatters: Magic is a key resource that makes quantum computers more powerful than classical computers, and knowing where it hides helps identify hard computational problems.
bite.eli5: Just like heavy objects take up more space, quantum systems have properties like entanglement and magic. This paper shows that some quantum states are easy to simulate, while others hide a complex kind of magic that overwhelms standard computers.

glossary.shortDef: A measure of how difficult a quantum state is to simulate using classical computers.
glossary.eli5Def: A measure of how deeply weird and un-simulatable a quantum system is.

glossary.shortDef: A scaling rule where entanglement grows with the surface area rather than the volume of a region.
glossary.eli5Def: A rule where the complexity of a system depends only on its outer boundary rather than its total guts.

glossary.shortDef: The lowest possible energy state of a quantum mechanical system.
glossary.eli5Def: The most relaxed, lowest-energy state a quantum system can settle into.
